prose_changes.old: It survived, which was not obvious in 1799. The Revolution stripped away the wealth and political entanglement that had defined the church for centuries, and what emerged after 1815 was poorer, more clerical and far more oriented toward Rome. The ultramontane Catholicism of the nineteenth century is the direct product of this catastrophe. The suppression and restoration of the Jesuits, the loss of the church lands, and the concordat as a way of settling with a secular state all set terms the church has operated under ever since. Its parish churches, seminaries and religious orders across Europe are still, physically, largely those of this period.
prose_changes.new: It survived, which was not obvious in 1799. The Revolution stripped away the wealth and political ties that had defined the church for centuries. What came out after 1815 was poorer, more clerical and far more turned toward Rome. The same line of popes carried it into the nineteenth century, when Catholics looked to Rome as never before. How much this crisis shaped that later church is a judgment, not a recorded fact. The loss of the Jesuits and their return set terms the church still works under. So did the loss of church lands, and the concordat as a way to make peace with a secular state. Its parish churches, seminaries and religious orders across Europe are still, physically, largely those of this period.
prose_changes.reason: 'The ultramontane Catholicism of the nineteenth century is the direct product of this catastrophe' states a causal reading as fact; no vendored text or repo-cited secondary work supports it. The continuity itself is documented (Pius VII signed concordats in 1801 and 1817; continued-as link), so that is what the field now asserts, with the causal claim qualified. One long sentence also split. Whole field rewritten; every other fact kept.
